abstract: Highlights Colorectal cancer metastasis, especially liver metastasis, is characterized by significant intricate diversity and remains a major contributor to patient mortality. Despite its clinical importance, the precise molecular mechanisms driving metastasis remain poorly understood. To investigate molecular drivers of metastasis heterogeneity, we performed a comprehensive proteomic analysis of non-metastatic (NM) colorectal cancer tissues, metachronous (MM) and synchronous (SM) metastatic tissues. Our analysis revealed distinct biological features associated with colorectal cancer liver metastasis. We identified P53-mediated hyperproliferation as a common initiating factor in the occurrence of CRC. Additionally, metabolic dysregulation emerged as a key hallmark of CRC liver metastasis. MM tumors exhibited suppressed ferroptosis and activation of the TGF-β signaling pathway, while SM tumors displayed inhibited anoikis and activation of the WNT signaling pathway, accompanied by activated angiogenesis. Most strikingly, CEACAM6 was identified as the only protein exhibiting a stepwise decrease in expression from NM to MM and further to SM, underscoring its unique role in metastatic progression. These findings provide new insights into the molecular complexities underpinning colorectal cancer liver metastasis..

Materials and methods
Sample collection
CRC tumor and CRC tumor adjacent para-cancerous sample (PN) were collected from patients clinically diagnosed non-metastasis CRC (NM), synchronous CRLM (SM) or metachronous CRLM (MM) at the Affiliated Zhongshan Hospital of Dalian University. Informed consents were obtained from all individual participants included in the study. This study was approved by the Ethical Committee of the Affiliated Zhongshan Hospital of Dalian University (Ref: KY2023–002–1).
Protein extraction
All samples were grinded with liquid nitrogen and kept on ice for 20 mins in lysis buffer (8 M urea, 100 mM NH₄HCO₃, pH 8.0) supplemented with protease inhibitors (Roche, USA). The lysate underwent sonication using a high-intensity ultrasonic processor at intervals of 1 s on and 1 s off, with a total processing time of 3 min and a power of 80 W. The sonicated samples were centrifuged at 15,000 g for 15 min to remove insoluble debris. This process was repeated to further eliminate any residual precipitates. The protein concentration was determined using a BCA assay kit (Beyotime Biotechnology, China) in accordance with the manufacturer’s protocol.
Protein digestion
100 mg total protein extract was incubated with 120 μl of reducing buffer (10 mM DTT, 8 M Urea, 100 mM TEAB, pH 8.0) at 60 °C for 1 h. 50 mM IAA was added in the dark for an additional 40 min at room temperature. The solutions were centrifuged on filters at 12,000 rpm for 20 min at 4 °C, and diluted by adding 120 μl of 300 mM TEAB, followed by centrifugation at 12,000 rpm for 20 min, repeating this step twice. 100 μl of 300 mM TEAB and 3 μl of sequencing-grade trypsin (1 μg/μL) were added, and the solutions were incubated for digestion at 37 °C for 12 h, and the digested peptides were centrifuged at 12,000 rpm for 20 min. 50 μl of 200 mM TEAB was added and centrifuged again. The supernatant was collected and lyophilized.
4D Label-free mass spectrometer LC-MS/MS analysis
All analyses were performed using a QE mass spectrometer (Thermo, USA) equipped with an Easyspray source (Thermo, USA). Samples were loaded through a capillary trap column (100 μm × 2 cm, RP-C18, Thermo Fisher, USA) and then separated by a capillary analytical column (15 cm × 75 μm, RP-C18, Thermo Fisher, USA) on an EASY-nLCTM 1200 system (Thermo, USA). The flow rate was set 300 nL/min and linear gradient was applied as follow: 0∼40 min, 5–30 % B;40∼55 min, 30–50 % B;55∼60 min, 50–100 % B. Full MS scans were acquired in the mass range of 300–1600 m
/z
with a mass resolution of 70,000, and the AGC target value was set at 1e6. The 10 most intense peaks in MS were subjected to fragmentation using higher-energy collisional dissociation (HCD) with a collision energy of 28. MS/MS spectra were obtained with a resolution of 35,000, an AGC target of 2e5, and a maximum injection time of 80 ms. Dynamic exclusion was set for 15.0 s, and the run was performed under positive mode.
Database search and protein quantification
The LC-MS/MS raw data were imported into MaxQuant software and processed using the Andromeda search engine. Tandem mass spectra were searched against the human SwissProt database (20,422 entries). To minimize the occurrence of peak matches by chance, a target-decoy-based false discovery rate (FDR) approach was employed. For peptide identification, the mass and intensity of peptide peaks in mass spectrometry (MS) spectra were detected and assembled into three-dimensional (3D) peak hills over the
m/z
retention time plane. These were then filtered using graph theory algorithms to identify isotope patterns. High mass accuracy was achieved through weighted averaging and mass recalibration, where the systematic mass error was subtracted from the measured mass of each MS isotope pattern. The peptide and fragment masses (in the case of MS/MS spectra) were searched against an organism-specific sequence database and scored using a probability-based approach known as the peptide score. The subsequent step involved the assembly of peptide hits into protein hits for protein identification, where each identified peptide of a protein contributed to the overall identification accuracy. The organism-specific database search included target sequences, their reverse counterparts, and contaminants to establish a statistical cutoff for acceptable spectral matches, thereby aiding in the determination of a false discovery rate (FDR) adjusted to <1 %. Identified proteins were required to include one or more unique peptides. The label-free quantification (LFQ) intensity of each protein in different samples was centrally transformed to obtain the relative quantitative value of the protein across various samples
Mass spectrometry quality control detection and sample repeatability test
A series of quality control evaluations including peptide length distribution, peptide number distribution, protein coverage distribution, and protein molecular weight distribution were performed to ensure the quality of mass spectrometry data. And the quantitative repeatability of samples was tested by three statistical analysis methods, including Pearson’s correlation coefficient (PCC), principal component analysis (PCA) and coefficient of variation (CV).
Bioinformatic analyses
Protein annotation was obtained from the UniProt-GOA database and the PANTHER classification system using ProteinPilot software. Following the central transformation of the label-free quantification (LFQ) intensity for each protein, the resulting relative protein intensities demonstrated normal distribution across all samples. To identify proteins specifically dysregulated in metachronous or synchronous liver metastasis of CRC tissue, we employed a Student's
t
-test to discern differentially expressed proteins (DEPs) between non-metastatic, metachronous, or synchronous metastatic tissue and para-tumor normal colorectal tissues. We applied a cutoff of 2-fold change with a P-value <0.05. The dysregulated proteins were then subjected to Gene Ontology (GO) analysis and KEGG pathway analysis using DAVID (
http://david.ncifcrf.gov
). Cluster analysis and PCA analysis was using R package factoextra (eclust and prcomp function), t-SNE using R package Rtsne, heatmap was using R package pheatmap, ridge plot and scatter plot using R package ggplot, survival plot using GEPIA2 (
http://gepia2.cancer-pku.cn/#index
) [
19
], PPI interaction plot using (
https://genemania.org/
) [
20
].
Immunohistochemistry
Paraffin-embedded sections were subjected to antigen retrieval with 0.01 M sodium citrate buffer (pH 6.0) at 90 °C, blocked with 5 % bovine serum albumin (BSA), incubated with primary antibody overnight at 4 °C, washed, incubated with secondary antibody at 37 °C for 1 hour, washed with PBS, stained with Diaminobenzidine (DAB), imaged by light microscope (Nikon, Ni-U). The CEACAM6 antibody (Cell Signaling Technology, USA) was used for immunohistochemistry experiments.
RNA extraction and RT-qPCR
Total RNA was extracted from freshly frozen CRC tumor tissues using TRIzol reagent using the TRIeasy™ Total RNA Extraction Reagent (Yeasen), precipitated, washed with 70 % ethanol, and dissolved in water. 1 μg of total RNA was reverse transcribed using random hexamers and Hiscript III Reverse Transcriptase (Vazyme). 20 ng cDNA was used in each RT-qPCR reaction on a CFX96 instrument using Taq Pro Universal SYBR qPCR Master Mix (Vazyme). All expression values were scaled to GAPDH. The genespecific primers (forward primer; reverse primer) used in all PCR-based analyses are: Human CEACAM6 (TCAATGGGACGTTCCAGCAAT; CACTCCAATCGTGATGCCGA); Human GAPDH (GGCTGAGAACGGGAAGCTTGTCAT; CAGCCTTCTCCATGGTGGTGAAGA).

Introduction

,

,
[11]

12
,
14
,

A comprehensive understanding of these molecular disparities holds the key to advancing personalized therapeutic strategies and refining prognostic assessments in the management of colorectal cancer liver metastasis [

Our comprehensive proteomic dataset revealed distinct molecular features associated with the heterogeneity of CRLM that could enhance our understanding of the molecular underpinnings of colorectal cancer liver metastasis and holds promise for refining diagnostic and therapeutic strategies tailored to specific metastatic profiles.

Results
Proteomic characterization of CRLM samples
To investigate the molecular classification of CRC metastasis heterogeneity, we conducted a high-resolution proteomic analysis on 20 CRC patients’ samples, including PN, NM, SM, and MM tissues (
Fig. 1
A). Clinical and pathological characteristics of these tumors were examined using CT scans and biopsy-derived tissue section staining (
Fig. 1
B). Pathological examination identified significant cellular atypia across all tumor samples, characterized by enlarged nuclei, an increased nuclear-cytoplasmic ratio, hyperchromasia, nuclear membrane thickening, prominent nucleoli, and elevated mitotic activity. The degree of differentiation distinguished tumor types: SM samples predominantly formed solid nests, indicating poorly differentiated adenocarcinoma; NM samples displayed glandular-like structures, representing well-differentiated adenocarcinoma; and MM samples exhibited an intermediate tissue morphology, signifying moderately differentiated adenocarcinoma.
Fig. 1
Proteomic characterization of CRLM samples.
(A) Summary of the proteomics workflow applied to colon cancer. Following tissue lysis and homogenization, purified and analysis. Data were analyzed and quantified in MaxQuant. (B) Validation by IHC and CT scans to confirm the type of colon cancer. (C) Number of quantified proteins were quantified. (D) Barplots showing the number of peptides with different molecular weight. (E)Cluster tree using protein quantity and clustered into 3 main groups. (F) t-distributed stochastic neighbor embedding (tSNE) representation of proteome for tumors and NATs, colored by samples. tSNE was based on features that were fully quantified across all samples.
Fig 1
LC-MS analysis successfully identified an average of 8000 proteins for each sample, with 2976 unique proteins detected in at least 15 of 20 samples (
Fig. 1
C). The molecular weight distribution analysis demonstrated a normal distribution of proteins ranging from 10 KD to 200 KD (
Fig. 1
D), indicating the robustness of the MS processing pipeline. To assess the similarities among these 20 samples, we performed hierarchical clustering based on Pearson correlation. As expected, tumor samples formed a distinct cluster, separate from PN samples. Surprisingly, SM samples were more closely related to NM than to MM samples (
Fig. 1
E). t-SNE analysis further confirmed that CRC tumors are molecularly distinct from normal tissues, with SM samples exhibiting closer proximity to NM than MM (
Fig. 1
F), implying that SM samples are at an earlier stage of transformation, while MM tumors may undergo unique molecular changes that prime them for metastasis at a later stage. These data identify important molecular distinctions between different CRC types based on their metastatic potential or disease progression timeline.
Proteomics features in CRC tumor tissues compared with PNs
To identify proteins specifically dysregulated in CRC tumors, we conducted a comparative analysis of differentially expressed proteins (DEPs) in SM, MM, and NM samples relative to PN tissues. We observed 198 upregulated proteins (
Fig. 2
A) and 99 downregulated proteins (
Fig. 2
B) across all CRC samples compared to PN samples. Gene Ontology (GO) and KEGG (Kyoto Encyclopedia of Genes and Genomes) analysis revealed that upregulated proteins were predominantly associated with P53 signaling, DNA repair (INO80B, MDC1, RRM1, UHRF1, PARP2, EYA3, NUDT1, CSNK1E, POLA1, CHAF1B, SUMO1, UBE2T, HSF1, CDK1, ERCC6, ATR), translation (RPS25, RPS17, RPS19, RPS29, RPL37A, DHPS, RPL35, RPL13, RPL29, RSL24D1, RPL17, MRPL57), rRNA processing (UTP25, DDX27, UTP23, RRP1, DDX21, DDX54, BYSL, NOL6, FTSJ3, BOP1, RPS25, RPS17, RPS19, NOB1, LYAR, RRP15), cell cycle regulation (SUV39H2, CGREF1, MDC1, MCM7, UHRF1, CDCA5, CDCA8, MKI67, CHTF18, ARPP19, CHAF1B, CCPG1, PSME3, MCM3, MCM4, HMG20B), ribosomal small subunit biogenesis (RPS25, RPS17, NOB1, RPS19, NGDN, NOL6), cell proliferation (BOP1, KAT2A, MCM7, BRAT1, FPGS, CDK1, MKI67, BYSL, BCL2L1), DNA replication (POLA1, CHAF1B, RRM1, MCM7, GINS3, DSCC1, SDE2, CDK1, MCM4, CHTF18, ATR), RNA methylation (METTL2B, NOP2, NSUN6, FTSJ3), and chromatin remodeling (KDM5A, INO80B, SUV39H2, KAT2A, ING3, EYA3, SMYD2, CDK1, DDX21, SOX9, ERCC6, TTI1). In contrast, the downregulated proteins were enriched in cGMP-PKC signaling (PDE3A, ATP2A3, ITPR1, ATP2B4, PDE5A, MYL9, MYLK), calcium signaling pathways, and aging (KRT16, IGFBP2, DMD, PCK1, FGF2) (
Fig. 2
C). These findings indicate a shift from normal cellular homeostasis towards a state of hyperproliferation, metabolic reprogramming, and evasion of growth suppressors, all hallmarks of oncogenic transformation and CRC progression.
Fig. 2
Proteomics Features in Tumor Tissues Compared with PNs.
(A)VENN plot showing the overlapped differential upregulated protein compared with para-tumor normal colorectal tissues (PN). (B) VENN plot showing the overlapped differential downregulated protein compared with para-tumor normal colorectal tissues. (C) Ridges plot showing the protein expression (log2(C/PN+1)) enriched GO iterms. (D) Heatmap showing differential expression protein among PN, NM, MM and SM group. (E) Heatmap showing differential expression protein among PN, NM, MM and SM group.
Fig 2
We further analyzed the uniquely expressed proteins in each CRC subtype, revealing distinct patterns when compared to PN samples. In NM samples, upregulated proteins were associated with DNA replication, mRNA processing, protein translation, and cell cycle regulation, while downregulated proteins were enriched in B cell-mediated immune response. Notably, all IGLV proteins, responsible for generating diverse antibodies in B cells, were downregulated, suggesting a metastasis-promoting role for B cells in CRC. Additionally, downregulated proteins included key regulators of the PPAR signaling pathway (APOA1, FABP3, FABP4, and FABP2) and Rap1 signaling pathway (PAR1B, GANQ, PFN2, TLN2, CSF1R, and MAP2K6). Different from NM, MM samples exhibited upregulation of proteins associated with the activation of innate immune response (ZBP1, NQO1, MX2, CASP4, MX1, SLC15A3, MBL2), activation of type 1 interferon response (SP100, MX1), and metabolic pathways (NQO1, ALDH1L1, NNMT, ELOVL5, PLAAT3, MAT1A, ASH1L, FMO4, GCAT, SELENOI, TYMP, SDR16C5, ADH4, ACADL, ADI1, KYNU, RDH16, UGT2B4, GLUL, ACOT4) (
Fig. 2
D). Downregulated proteins were associated with cell adhesion (FER, PRKCE, DSC2, FARP2, COL28A1, TGFB1L1, EMILIN1, and LSAMP) and focal adhesion (VCL, PRKCA, FLNA, FLNC, PPP1R12C, PPP1R12B, and MYL12B), suggesting that MM tumors exhibit a loss of adhesion and ECM remodeling, which primes them for metastasis. However, the enhanced immune surveillance observed in these tumors may inhibit right away metastatic progression. In contrast, in SM tumors, angiogenesis key repressors COL15A1, HSPG2, MEIS1, NRCAM, and SCG2, cell adhesion molecules AZGP1, PTPRS, CDHR5, and FLG2, and extracellular matrix (ECM) organization factors ELN, PTX3, and ADAMTSL4 were significatedly downregulated, suggesting a shift in the tumor microenvironment that supports vascularization and sustained growth of metastatic lesions, reflecting clinical hallmarks of SM (
Fig. 2
E).
We conclude that CRC development is characterized by dysregulation of the P53 signaling pathway and metabolic reprogramming. Each CRC subtype (NM, SM, MM) exhibits a distinct protein expression profile, reflecting the heterogeneity of molecular mechanisms contributing to CRC progression.
Proteomics features in CRLM compared with Non-CRLM
To elucidate proteins implicated in CRLM metastasis, we compared the DEPs which identified MM vs NM and SM vs NM. Comparison between MM and NM groups, a total of 235 upregulated proteins and 238 downregulated proteins (
Fig. 3
A). These upregulated proteins are more associated with metabolic pathways and glycosphingolipid biosynthesis, including prominent candidates such as UGT2A3, NCOA1, CA8, and ALDH1A1, while the downregulated proteins are associated with peroxisome and ferroptosis (TFRC, SLC11A2, ACSL6, and ACSL5) and, suggesting ferroptosis suppression provides a survival advantage in the harsh metastatic microenvironment for MM. Importantly, PPAR regulators (FABP6, HMGCS1) and TGF-β signaling pathways regulators (SMAD3, TGIF1, TFDP1, and SMURF2) were also downregulated, which together explain the enhanced metastasis potential of MM (
Fig. 3
B).
Fig. 3
Proteomics Features in CRLM Compared with Non-CRLM.
(A) Scatter plot showing the differential expression protein between NM and MM group. (B)Heatmap showing the differential protein between NM and MM group and their enriched pathway and GO items. (C) Scatter plot showing the differential expression protein between NM and SM. (D) Heatmap showing the differential protein between NM and SM group and their enriched pathway and GO items. (E) Venn plot showing differential highly expressed protein in two groups including SM and MM compared with NM separately. (F) Heatmap showing the overlapped protein and their enriched pathway and GO items. (G) Venn plot showing differential decreased expressed protein in two groups including SM and MM compared with NM separately. (H) Heatmap showing the overlapped protein and their enriched pathway and GO items. (I) Over survival using protein (AXL, ACSL6, PMEPA1, BCL2L1, AKR1C2, RBP5) to predict patient’s survival rate.
Fig 3
When compared between SM and NM groups, 102 upregulated and 102 downregulated proteins (
Fig. 3
C) were identified. Similarly, SM samples exhibited a broad activation of metabolic pathways. However, downregulation of the IL-17 signaling pathway regulators (MMP3, PTGS2, and S100A9) and promoting neutrophil extracellular trap formation (AZU1, HMGB1, MPO and ELANE) in SM samples were observed, indicating a less inflammatory microenvironment that facilitates more advanced metastatic progression. Remarkably, CEACAM6 and BCL2L1, the negative regulators of anoikis, a distinct cell death type, were downregulated in the SM group, suggesting that SM samples are adapting to a less inflammatory, more metabolically active state, where they can evade immune responses and avoid anoikis during metastasis (
Fig. 3
D).
Further investigation into common events associated with colon cancer liver metastasis involved overlapping the differentially expressed proteins between MM vs NM and SM vs NM analyses. This revealed 36 upregulated proteins (including NCOA1, HLA-DRB4, CA8, ADH1B, ALDH1A1) (
Fig. 3
E and
3
F) and 23 downregulated proteins (including ARID3A) (
Fig. 3
G and
3
H) in CRLM samples. Enrichment analysis of the activated overlapped proteins demonstrated their association with various metabolic pathways, while upregulated proteins are associated with Gene Ontology (GO) results indicated enrichment in retinol metabolic, xenobiotics metabolic, and prostaglandin metabolic pathways. In contrast, downregulated proteins were associated with processes such as epithelial cell proliferation, amino acid transport, negative regulation of anoikis, negative regulation of dendritic cell apoptotic processes, and the vascular endothelial growth factor (VEGF) receptor signaling pathway, confirming that metabolic reprogramming and inhibition of angiogenesis is the common feature of metastasis.
The current central clinical concern revolves around predicting the potential risk of metastasis in initially non-metastatic MM and SM patients [
5
,
21
,
22
]. Considering the observed shorter survival time in CRC patients with metastasis [
23
], we conducted an assessment of the correlation between the expression of overlapped proteins (36 upregulated and 23 downregulated, as shown in
Fig. 3
E and
3
G) and survival duration. Initial findings did not reveal significant differences in individual factors, but through further analysis, we generated survival curves for various protein combinations. Notably, a subset of proteins (AXL, ACSL6, PMEPA1, BCL2L1, AKR1C2, RBP5) showed a significant correlation with poor prognosis in patients (
p
< 0.05) (
Fig. 3
I). This subset may potentially serve as an indicator to predict the metastasis potential in these patients.
In summary, these findings underscore metabolic dysregulation as a predominant hallmark of colon cancer liver metastasis. However, the diverse signaling pathways involved in the immune response, and the inhibition of specific cell death types, and angiogenesis activation, may serve as crucial determinants in the metastatic type.
Proteomics features in SM compared with MM
To further analyze the molecular basis of heterogeneity in CRC metastasis, a comparison of DEPs between SM and MM was performed. This analysis revealed 149 upregulated proteins (including PTMS, FUT2) and 160 downregulated proteins (including SEMAG, TFF1, IFT140) between SM and MM groups (
Fig. 4
A). Notably, TGF-beta signaling was found to be highly activated in the SM group, suggesting its potential role in the promote metastatic behavior. Simultaneously, canonical WNT signaling pathway showed positive regulation, accompanied by significant chromatin organization changes in SM samples (
Fig. 4
B).
Fig. 4
Proteomics Features in SM Compared with MM.
(A) Scatter plot showing the differential expression protein between SM and MM group. (B) Heatmap showing the differential protein between SM and MM group and their enriched pathway and GO items. (C) PPI interaction analysis revealed a sub-network of proteins that displayed distinct co-expression patterns in SM patients, where purple connections indicate co-expression between proteins, red connections indicate physical interaction, blue connections indicate co-localization in SM samples. Proteins with red dotted circles are involved in secretory granule lumen, with blue dotted are involved in humoral immune response and with yellow dotted are involved in hydrogen peroxide metabolic process.
Fig 4
To further elucidate the effects of these metastasis-associated proteins and provide insights into the interplay and potential collaborative functions of the dysregulated proteins, differential dependency network analysis was constructed to identify node genes that differentially expressed in the SM and MM group connected to genes linked to increased CRC risk including FUT2 with higher expression in CRC tissues, AGT serves as a potential biomarker and drives tumor progression in colorectal carcinoma, and MPO, increased in colorectal cancer with a poor prognosis. These nodes had different signaling connections in SM and MM group. These data offer a nuanced exploration of the protein landscape associated with metachronous and synchronous liver metastasis in CRC tissue, shedding light on potential key players and signaling pathways driving the observed heterogeneity.
To enhance our comprehension of the impact of metastasis-associated proteins and gain insights into the interplay and potential collaborative functions of dysregulated proteins, a protein network analysis was conducted to identify proteins with a fold change of <0.4) that were differentially expressed in the SM group. The protein related to the secretory granule lumen, humoral immune response, and hydrogen peroxide metabolic process were connected to proteins associated with increased CRC metastasis (
Fig. 4
C). These findings offer a nuanced exploration of the protein landscape linked to metachronous and synchronous liver metastasis in CRC tissue. This approach illuminates potential key players and signaling pathways that contribute to the observed heterogeneity in the context of metastasis.
Proteomic markers associated with the degree of metastasis in CRLM
To further explore the functional implications of these dysregulated proteins and their roles in defining the metastatic characteristics of CRLM, we systematically identified proteins consistently upregulated (
Fig. 5
A) or downregulated (
Fig. 5
B) across the NM, MM, and SM groups. Using pie chart overlap analysis, we unexpectedly identified CEACAM6 as the only protein exhibiting significantly elevated expression in SM compared to MM and, further, to NM groups. This finding underscores that MM and SM metastases arise through distinct mechanisms, rather than differences in metastasis extent or timing. CEACAM6 expression was found to be very high in NM samples (
Fig. 5
C). To validate these proteomic findings at the transcriptional and histological levels, we performed RT-qPCR and IHC analysis of patient tumor tissues. Both mRNA expression and staining intensity closely mirrored the proteomic results, with NM samples exhibiting the strongest CEACAM6 signal, followed by MM and SM groups (
Fig. 5
D–E). Collectively, these results identify CEACAM6 as a pivotal determinant in the metastatic continuum of CRLM.

Discussion
Despite significant strides in the diagnosis and treatment of colon cancer, a notable gap remains in our comprehension of the heterogeneity underlying colon cancer liver metastasis [
2
]. Our research has revealed that P53-mediated hyperproliferation plays a pivotal role as a common trigger in the development of colon cancer. Moreover, we have identified metabolic dysregulation as a prevalent hallmark in the context of colon cancer liver metastasis. Remarkable findings include the activation of TGF-beta and WNT signaling pathways, coupled with substantial changes in chromatin organization. These molecular events are likely contributors to the observed malignant heterogeneity in colon cancer metastasis.
Our data strongly suggest that dysregulation of P53 signaling is a common feature in the occurrence of CRC. P53, considered one of the least studied tumor suppressors, is found to be mutated or deleted in over half of human tumors [
24
]. In human colorectal tumors, wild-type p53 alleles are frequently lost due to mutations, deletions, or a combination of both [
25
,
26
]. P53 mutation in CRC occurs in 34 % of proximal colon tumors and 45 % of distal colorectal tumors [
27
]. Notably, in all examined NM, MM, and SM samples, the expression of key molecules of P53, including MDM2 and MDMX, are impaired. As a negative regulator, MDM2 facilitates the binding of the transactivation domain (TAD) of the P53 protein [
28
]. We posit that P53 signaling likely acts as a safeguard to inhibit carcinogenesis in CRC, suggesting that all CRC patients could potentially benefit from therapies targeting P53 signaling [
29
,
30
], pending confirmation of specific molecules with fewer side effects.
The finding that dysregulation in metabolic pathways, particularly involving retinol metabolic pathways, xenobiotics metabolic pathways, and prostaglandin metabolic pathways, contributes to colon cancer liver metastasis is noteworthy. Previous reports have suggested that cancer cells adapt their metabolism to counter cancer-associated cellular stress [
31
,
32
]. Notably, studies have indicated a robust correlation between retinol intake or blood retinol levels and cancer risk, attributing this effect to the disruption of retinol-mediated suppression of tumor-promoting IL-6 in neoplastic tissue [
33
]. Changes in the composition of gut microbiota could be a primary factor in the deregulation of xenobiotic metabolism [
34
]. Moreover, CRC progression is associated with an elevation in prostaglandin biosynthesis, particularly systemic TXA2 biosynthesis [
35
]. We posit that such metabolic reprogramming may facilitate the metastasis process by evading immune response activity [
[36]
,
[37]
,
[38]
,
[39]
], highlighting the importance of considering metabolic pathways in the context of colon cancer liver metastasis.
Finally, we found that the malignancy of CRLM is governed by the activation of TGF-beta and WNT signaling, accompanied by concurrent chromatin remodeling. Prior studies have proposed that TGF-beta-stimulated cancer-associated fibroblasts (CAFs) trigger GP130/STAT3 signaling in tumor cells [
40
]. Additionally, WNT signaling activation in CRC occurs through the inactivation of APC or mutation of β-catenin, promoting the nuclear accumulation of β-catenin [
41
]. This, in turn, induces epithelial-mesenchymal transition (EMT) progression by altering cell-cell connections, contributing to the aggressiveness of CRC [
[41]
,
[42]
,
[43]
]. Clinical datasets have also identified a crucial chromatin remodeling axis, where hepatic growth factor (HGF) induces phosphorylation of PU.1 [
[44]
,
[45]
,
[46]
]. Based on these findings, we propose that these signaling pathways may stimulate cancer epigenome reprogramming, inducing cancer cell stemness and activating the metastasis process. This aligns with a hypothesized 'cancer stem cell' model of colon cancer [
[47]
,
[48]
,
[49]
], where hyperactivation of TGF-beta and WNT signaling induces epigenome reprogramming, fostering cancer cell stemness via positive feedback loops and thereby enhancing the metastatic potential. The expression of CEACAM6 may be dynamically regulated in response to tumor progression stages or changes in the microenvironment, with cancer cells potentially downregulating CEACAM6 during the metastatic process to adapt to the new microenvironment. Also, reduced expression of CEACAM6 may assist tumor cells in evading immune surveillance, thereby providing a competitive advantage during the metastatic process.
Conclusions
In summary, the differentially expressed proteins (DEPs) between synchronous and metachronous metastasis were identified through a high-throughput proteomics approach. These proteins may serve as key components underlying the observed heterogeneity in CRC metastasis and warrant further in-depth investigation to elucidate their molecular functions and potential clinical implications.
